# How to Remove Personal Details From a Document Before Using an AI Tool

> **In short:** You can keep the useful content of a document and hide the personal details by replacing names, account numbers and addresses with neutral placeholders like "Person One." Always check the result yourself, because a detail you missed stays visible to the chatbot.

Many people paste a letter, bill or work file into an AI chatbot and ask for a summary or a rewrite. That can be very helpful, but documents often contain details you would not want to share. In this guide you will make a safe working copy, build a private list of what to hide, swap in placeholders, and check the result before anything leaves your computer. By the end, you will have a version the chatbot can work with, and you will know how to put the real details back yourself.

## Before you start

- **A document you want help with**, saved on your computer or in a cloud service such as Google Docs or Microsoft Word.
- **Any AI chatbot account** you already use, or a free one. The placeholder method works the same way in every tool.
- **A blank notes file** (Notepad, Notes, or any plain text app) for your private list. It must stay on your device and never go into the chatbot.
- **About 15 to 20 minutes.** Longer documents take more time to check.

## Step 1 — Make a working copy of the document

Never edit your original. Open the document and save a second copy first. Most word processors let you do this from the file menu, usually under a name like "Save as" or "Make a copy." If you cannot find it, check your program's help center, or simply copy the file in your file manager and paste it back into the same folder.

Give the copy a clear name, such as "bill-working-copy." Once it opens, you should see the same text and layout as the original, with the new name shown at the top of the window.

💬 Example: Name the copy "letter-working-copy" so you never confuse it with the file that holds the real details.

You'll know it worked when you have two files, and the one you are editing has the new name.

## Step 2 — Write a private list of what to hide

Read the document once from start to finish. Every time you notice something that identifies a person, an account or a place, write it in your notes file. Include full names, first names used alone, email addresses, phone numbers, street addresses, account or policy numbers, dates of birth and ID numbers. Do not forget smaller clues, such as the name of a school your child attends or a company unique to one employer.

Give each item a simple label, such as "Person One = Maria Lopez." This list is the key that lets you restore the real details later, so keep it on your device only.

If the document is long, go one page at a time. When you are not sure whether something is personal, add it to the list anyway. Extra caution costs you nothing.

💬 Example: Write in your notes: "Person One = Maria Lopez, Account A = [your account number]."

You'll know it worked when your list covers every name, number and address you noticed on the first read-through.

## Step 3 — Replace each detail with a placeholder

Most word processors and office programs have a search tool that can also swap one piece of text for another. Its exact name and location vary by program, so if you cannot find it quickly, search your program's help center for "find and replace." Use it to work through your list one item at a time.

Type the first item from your list exactly as it appears in the document, then type its placeholder in the matching box. Apply the change to every match. Use placeholders that are obviously fake, such as "Person One," "Account A" or "123 Sample Street," so you can spot them later.

Be consistent. If "Maria" and "Maria Lopez" both appear, handle both. If you are not sure the tool catches every version, search for each spelling separately.

💬 Example: Replace "Maria Lopez" with "Person One" everywhere it appears in the working copy.

You'll know it worked when a search for the original name finds nothing, and the placeholder appears wherever the name used to be.

## Step 4 — Check the hidden corners

Replacing text in the main body is not always enough. Many documents hide personal details where you do not normally look. Check the headers and footers at the top and bottom of each page, which often carry a name, a phone number or a file path. Check comments and tracked changes, which show who edited the file. Check the signature block at the end of a letter, and any logo or image that contains text.

Many programs also store author and company names in a file information panel. Look for a section called "Info" or "Properties" in your program's file menu, and clear any personal names you find there. If you are not sure where it is, the help center will show you.

Finally, rename the file itself. The file name is often the first thing an AI tool sees.

💬 Example: Rename "Maria-Lopez-bill-March" to "bill-working-copy" before you upload anything.

You'll know it worked when you have scrolled through every header, footer and comment, and none of them show a real name or number.

## Step 5 — Read the result yourself, then share it

Read the cleaned document slowly, from start to finish. Ask yourself whether someone could identify the person, the account or the place from what remains. Watch for clues that are not names, such as a rare job title, a unique street, or a story only one family would recognize. Replace any such clue with a general description, like "a local school."

Next, search once more for each original item on your list and confirm zero results. Then search for the @ symbol and for long strings of digits. Any hits deserve a second look.

Now open your AI chatbot, start a new conversation, and paste in the cleaned text. Before you do, look in the tool's settings or help pages for privacy or data-control options, and read how that company describes its handling of conversations in its own words. A tool cannot guarantee anonymity; it can only help you hide what you can see, so your own reading is the real safety step.

When the answer comes back, use your private list to put the real names back in your own copy. The chatbot never needs to see them. Remember that chatbots can make mistakes, so check any important answer against your original file.

💬 Example: "Here is a cleaned-up letter where names and numbers are replaced with placeholders like Person One. Summarize the main points in [number] short bullet points."

You'll know it worked when the chatbot's answer makes sense using the placeholders, and you can match each one back to your private list.

## Common mistakes

- **Forgetting headers, footers, comments and file names.** These often repeat the same personal details as the body text. Fix it by checking every page edge, every comment and the file name in Step 4.
- **Replacing only one spelling.** If a name appears as "Maria," "M. Lopez" and "Maria Lopez," a single search misses some of them. Fix it by searching for each version separately, then searching once more to confirm nothing is left.
- **Pasting your private list into the chat.** If you share the key, the whole process is undone. Fix it by keeping the list in a notes file on your device, and never copying it into a prompt.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** Before asking a chatbot to explain a medical bill, a lease or a school letter, swap the names and numbers for placeholders first. You still get a clear explanation, and your family's details stay with you.
- **For your business or work:** Before sharing a customer list, a contract draft or an internal report with an AI tool, follow the same steps. Also check your employer's rules about which tools are approved, since those rules come from your workplace, not from this guide.
- **If you're just getting started:** Practice on a short, non-sensitive document first, such as a recipe with a family name in it, until the find-and-replace routine feels comfortable.

## Try it now

Pick one document on your computer that contains a name or a number. Make a working copy, write down three personal details in your notes file, and replace them with placeholders. Then read the first paragraph once more and confirm that nothing real remains. That is the whole habit, and it takes about two minutes.
